title: Event-Driven Architecture Fundamentals
description: Learn the fundamentals of event-driven architecture and its benefits for microservices.

data.text: Event-driven architecture (EDA) is a paradigm where services communicate through events rather than direct calls. LinkedIn, Netflix, and Uber process billions of events daily using event-driven patterns to achieve loose coupling and high scalability.

In EDA, producers publish events to an event broker, and consumers subscribe to events they care about. Producers do not know who is listening, and consumers do not know who produced the event. This enables loose coupling and independent evolution.

data.title: Key Benefits
items: Loose coupling: Services do not know about each other
Scalability: Add or remove consumers without changing producers
Resilience: If a consumer is down, events persist in the broker
Audit trail: Event logs provide a complete history of system changes
Real-time processing: Consumers can react to events immediately

data.title: Real-World Example
data.text: Netflix uses event-driven architecture extensively. When you watch a show, events are published for recommendations, billing, content delivery, and analytics—all independently.

data.code: When an order is created, multiple services react independently.

items.question: Is event-driven architecture always better?
items.answer: No. It adds complexity with message brokers, event schemas, and eventual consistency. Use it when you need loose coupling and real-time processing.

items.question: What is an event broker?
items.answer: An event broker is middleware that routes and persists events. Kafka, RabbitMQ, and AWS EventBridge are popular choices.

items.question: How do I handle event ordering?
items.answer: Use partitioning keys to ensure events for the same entity are ordered. Kafka guarantees order within a partition.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Event brokers provide persistence and routing
EDA enables independent scaling and evolution
Use EDA when you need real-time processing and loose coupling
data.takeaway: Event-driven architecture is powerful for complex domains but requires careful event design and schema management.
